lesson.title: Smoothing the Histogram: What a Density Curve Really Represents
lesson.summary: A density curve is an idealized, smooth version of a histogram whose total area equals exactly 1, letting area under any portion of the curve represent the proportion of data in that range.
lesson.body:
Every histogram you have drawn depends on an arbitrary choice: how wide to make the bars. Narrow the bars and the outline gets jagged; widen them and you lose detail. A density curve solves this problem by imagining what happens as the bars get narrower and narrower while the sample size grows larger and larger: the jagged histogram outline smooths into a single continuous curve. That curve is a mathematical model of the distribution, the same distribution you have been describing with words like symmetric, skewed, or bimodal, except now it is captured as a precise mathematical object rather than a picture built from a particular dataset.

A density curve has to satisfy two strict rules to count as valid. First, it must never dip below the horizontal axis, since a negative height would imply a negative proportion of data, which is meaningless. Second, the total area trapped between the curve and the horizontal axis must equal exactly 1. That area of 1 represents all of the data, 100 percent of it, so the entire dataset is accounted for somewhere under the curve. These two rules apply to every density curve you will ever meet, whether it is shaped like a bell, a rectangle, or something lopsided.

The single most important idea to take from density curves is this: area under the curve, not height of the curve, represents proportion of data. The height at any one point tells you how densely values are packed near that point, but it does not by itself tell you what fraction of the data lies there. Only by measuring the area over an interval, essentially adding up an infinite number of infinitely thin slices, do you get a proportion you can actually use, such as the fraction of values below a certain score or between two bounds.

A simple example makes this concrete. Suppose a spinner lands anywhere from 0 to 10 with equal likelihood, so its density curve is a flat rectangle stretching from 0 to 10. Because the total area must equal 1 and the base of the rectangle has width 10, the height must be 1 divided by 10, or 0.1, since area equals base times height. To find the proportion of spins landing between 2 and 5, compute the area of the rectangle over that interval: width 3 times height 0.1, which equals 0.3. So 30 percent of spins are expected to land between 2 and 5, a number you got purely from area, without ever touching an actual dataset.

Density curves also clarify something that is easy to mix up in a skewed distribution: the median and the mean sit in different places. The median is the point that splits the area exactly in half, so half the area lies on each side, while the mean is the balance point of the curve, the spot where the curve would perfectly balance on a fingertip. In a right skewed curve, the long tail pulls the mean above the median, even though the median remains the fifty fifty area split. Keeping area, not just shape, in mind is exactly the skill you will build on next, when area under a curve becomes the tool for computing real probabilities.
